back: Returning a fraction of the output to the inverting input so that it opposes the change that produced it.
Lower gain, but stable and set by resistors; wider bandwidth; less distortion.
A point held at almost 0 V by feedback without being connected to 0 V (the inverting input of an inverting amplifier).
$G = 1 + \dfrac{R_f}{R_1}$ (output in phase; very high input resistance)
Output joined to the inverting input, input to the non-inverting input: gain 1. Used as a buffer between a weak source and a load.
Very large A₀ (not saturated) so V⁺ ≈ V⁻; very large input resistance so no current enters the inputs.
Gain × bandwidth ≈ constant (about 1 MHz for a 741): a gain of 100 gives about 10 kHz bandwidth.
If |G × V_in| exceeds the saturation voltage, the output is flat at ±V_sat: sine-wave peaks are clipped.
